papers.title: Approximating Minimum Spanning Trees in Metrics under Semi-Random Corruptions
papers.abstract: We study the problem of finding minimum spanning trees in semi-random corrupted metrics. In this problem proposed by Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), we start with a metric space $\mathcal{M} = (X, d)$. The adversary independently corrupts each pairwise distance with probability $p$. The algorithm only observes these possibly corrupted distances and must output a spanning tree whose expected cost (in the true metric) is multiplicatively close to the minimum spanning tree cost. Prior work showed that losing a factor of $Ω(\log n)$ is necessary, even if the algorithm may adaptively select $O(n/\log n)$ points and probe the true distances between them. However, no upper bounds were known. We study three regimes based on whether the adversary can only increase, decrease, or arbitrarily change the corrupted distances. We show the following: (1) In the increase-only setting, we give a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. (2) In the decrease-only setting, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. Additionally, we show an $O(\log^4 n)$-approximation algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time $n^{O(\log n)}$, for any constant $p \leq 0.1$. Moreover, we show that a polynomial-time algorithm computing an $n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$-approximation is unlikely to exist. (3) In the general setting, where the adversary can both increase and decrease distances, we show an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for every $0 \leq p < \frac{1}{4}$. Further, we show that no $o(n)$-approximation is possible for $\frac{1}{2} \leq p < 1$. Our algorithms answer the main open question in Bateni et al.'s work; moreover, the $O(\log n)$-approximations in the latter two settings are information-theoretically optimal.

papers.title: On Zeros and Algorithms for Disordered Systems II: The Antiferromagnetic Ising Model up to Kesten-Stigum
papers.abstract: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm to estimate the partition function of the antiferromagnetic Ising model on the uniformly random $d$-regular graph to arbitrarily high accuracy for all inverse temperatures up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold. This is the entire regime in which the model is "replica symmetric," and is conjectured to be optimal for polynomial-time counting and sampling. To achieve our algorithmic result, we establish the absence of Fisher zeros for the partition function in a constant-width strip around the interval from $0$ up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, with high probability over the randomness of the input graph. AI Disclosure: The overarching vision and proof architecture were developed solely by the authors without AI input. GPT 5.5 Pro was used, with extensive guidance from the authors, for only a few minor technical aspects of the proof. The authors independently verified correctness and wrote everything by hand. We take full responsibility for its contents. A more detailed statement can be found in Section 1.2.

papers.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
papers.abstract: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-\textsf{Majority}, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-\textsf{Majority} achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-\textsf{Majority} that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

papers.title: Communication-Oblivious Permutation and Sorting
papers.abstract: With the help of secure hardware such as trusted execution environments (TEEs), private data can be uploaded and computed in untrusted cloud clusters, so that an adversary controlling the cloud can only see the data in encrypted form. However, the communication pattern between the processors may still reveal sensitive information about the data, so it is important to develop parallel algorithms in the BSP model whose communication pattern is independent of the input data, a property known as \textit{communication obliviousness}. In this paper, we study such algorithms for three fundamental problems: permutation, sorting, and 0-1 sorting. For the first two problems, we prove a tight (up to lower-order terms) communication complexity of $(2-2/p)n\pm o(n)$. Here, $p$ is the number of processors and $n$ is the input size, assuming $2\le p$ and $p=o(n^{1/3})$. Our lower bound holds regardless of the number of rounds and local memory size, while for balanced permutation and sorting the upper bound is achieved in a constant number of rounds with load at most $n/p+o(n/p)$. For 0-1 sorting, we also derive a tight communication complexity of $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p) \cdot n \pm o(n)$, where $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p)$ is the optimal value of a linear program parameterized by $p$. Although there appears to be no closed-form for $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p)$, we show that it is strictly smaller than $2-2/p$ for all $p\ge 3$, thus separating 0-1 sorting from general sorting in terms of their communication complexity.

papers.title: Four-Coloring Planar Graphs in Linear Time
papers.abstract: The famous Four Color Theorem (4CT) states that any planar graph can be colored with four colors, but how do we find a 4-coloring? In our previous paper [FOCS'26], we presented a simple combinatorial algorithm to 4-color planar graphs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We improve it here to $O(n)$ time, which is optimal. The algorithm from our previous paper is based on proving that every planar triangulation has a linear number of reducible configurations or obstructing cycles. The bottleneck for the algorithm is that we need $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes to extend a recursive 4-coloring to the reducible configurations. Each Kempe change can involve a constant fraction of the graph and takes linear time. Here we show that all $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes can be identified and implemented in $O(n)$ time. The idea is to spend $O(n)$ time to preprocess the graph so that we can identify and simulate each good Kempe change in $O(n/\log n)$ amortized time. Thus, we implement all $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes in $O(n)$ total time. Based on this, we implement the whole 4-coloring in linear time. We note that creating such a representation for fast identification and simulation of the right Kempe changes is a challenge of data structures, unlike the previous paper that builds on a new graph theoretic understanding of reducible configurations.

papers.title: The Tight Competitive Ratio of Greedy for Online Steiner Forest
papers.abstract: The online Steiner Forest problem is a fundamental network design problem in which terminal pairs arrive one at a time and an algorithm must irrevocably purchase edges connecting each pair. The natural greedy algorithm connects each terminal pair by a shortest path after making all previously purchased edges free. Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal (SODA 1996) proved that this algorithm is $O(log^2 k)$-competitive and conjectured an $O(log k)$ bound, where $k$ is the number of terminal pairs. Bamas, Drygala, and Maggiori (SODA 2022) obtained an $O(\log \NumPairs\log\log \NumPairs)$ bound for greedy on a restricted class of inputs, leaving the general case open. In this paper, we resolve the competitive ratio of the greedy algorithm for online Steiner Forest, proving that it is tightly $Θ(log(k) log log(k))$. Specifically, we establish an $O(log(k) log log(k))$ upper bound for arbitrary instances and construct a matching $Ω(log(k) log log(k))$ lower bound. Our results refute the $O(log k)$ conjecture of Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal and establish a tight $Θ(log log k)$ separation between the greedy algorithm and the best possible online algorithm for Steiner Forest.

papers.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Size of Order Graphs
papers.abstract: Order graphs were introduced by Arroyuelo et al.\ (TODS 2024) as a generalization of the ring index, to support worst-case optimal joins on relations of arity $d$ while storing as few columns as possible: the index stores one column per edge, so its size is proportional to the number of edges of an order graph. It was known that the minimum number of edges lies between $Ω(2^d\sqrt d)$ and $O(2^d d)$, and the lower bound had been claimed to be $42$ for $d=6$. We first exhibit an order graph with only $40$ edges for $d=6$, and show that the proof of that lower bound holds only for unions of cycles, whereas order graphs can be smaller than the smallest set of cycles. We give a corrected statement and proof that holds for every order graph: there must be at least $\max_m\binom dm\lceil m/2\rceil$ edges. This bound is $40$ for $d=6$, so our $40$-edge graph is optimal. We then settle the asymptotic question: the minimum size is $Θ(2^d\sqrt d)$. This is obtained via an explicit construction, based on symmetric chain decompositions of the Boolean lattice, with at most $(d-1)\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}+2^d$ edges. The upper bound is within a factor $4+O(d^{-1/2})$ of the lower bound, and both numerically and asymptotically better than trie switching.

papers.title: First-Order Bilevel Optimization for Non-truthful Auction Design
papers.abstract: Automated mechanism design has enabled the learning of complex auction mechanisms using neural networks. However, designing non-truthful auctions remains challenging because bidders' equilibrium strategies depend on the auction mechanism and thus evolve as the mechanism is optimized. In this work, we formulate auction design as a Stackelberg game with multiple strategic followers and develop a fully first-order algorithm for revenue optimization in non-truthful auctions. We establish non-asymptotic guarantees for hypergradient approximation and show that, under standard smoothness and strong-monotonicity assumptions, our method reaches an $O(ε)$-stationary point using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(ε^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls. Experiments on symmetric and asymmetric single-item auctions, as well as multi-item auctions, show that our method converges faster than second- and zeroth-order baselines and scales better as the number of bidders increases. Our method also discovers auctions that achieve revenue close to truthful baselines. These results provide a scalable framework for automated mechanism design beyond truthful auctions.

papers.title: Half-Optimal Induced Matchings in Random Graphs: Online and Low-Degree Algorithms
papers.abstract: For many optimization problems on random graphs, most prominently the largest independent set problem, natural algorithms reach only half the optimum, and such factor-two gaps are known to be sharp within broad algorithmic classes. We prove such a gap for finding large induced matchings in Erdős-Rényi random graphs. In the worst case, requiring a matching to be induced turns a polynomial-time solvable problem into an NP-hard one; our results reveal an average-case counterpart. In $G(n,p)$ with $C/n\le p\le 1-κ$, the largest induced matching has size $(1+o(1))L$ with high probability, where $L=\log_{1/(1-p)}(np)$. A simple online greedy algorithm finds an induced matching of size $(1/2-ε)L$, while no online algorithm, even with adaptive inspection order and unbounded computation, finds one of size $(1/2+ε)L$ except with probability $\exp(-Ω(L\log(np)))$. In the sparse regime $p=d/n$, low-degree polynomial algorithms exhibit the same sharp threshold. Our guarantees rest on a maximality principle: with high probability, every maximal induced matching is half-optimal. Greedy outputs a maximal induced matching and our low-degree algorithm a near-maximal one. We bypass the delicate coupling arguments classically used to analyze greedy since Karp. For low-degree hardness, we adapt Wein's overlap gap argument, with forbidden structures that track overlaps between endpoint sets rather than edge sets, since a new edge may join two previously used endpoints and thus encounter no fresh randomness. For online hardness, we give a new and significantly simpler argument that avoids the correlated instances of prior OGP-based proofs: at a suitable stopping time, all pairs involving uninspected vertices remain unrevealed, so a direct first-moment bound suffices.

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Sparse Navigable Graphs in General Metrics
papers.abstract: We study approximation algorithms for constructing sparse navigable graphs in general metrics. Given an $n$-point metric $(P,d)$ and a parameter $α\ge1$, a directed graph on $P$ is $α$-navigable if, for every pair of distinct points $s,t\in P$, the source $s$ has an outgoing neighbor $p$ with $d(p,t)<d(s,t)/α$. The objective is to minimize the number of edges. Recent independent works of Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (2026) and Conway et al. (2026) give $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithms and show that an $o(\log n)$ approximation is NP-hard in general. Before our work, the best known running time for such an approximation for general $α\ge1$ was $\widetilde O(\min\{n\operatorname{OPT}_α,n^{2.5}\})$, where $\operatorname{OPT}_α$ is the minimum number of edges in an $α$-navigable graph. In this paper, we give a randomized algorithm that, with high probability, runs in $\widetilde O(n^2)$ time and achieves an $O(\log n)$ approximation for every $α\ge1$. In general, these guarantees are nearly optimal up to constant factors in the approximation and polylogarithmic factors in the running time.

papers.title: Uniform Capacitated Clustering with Few Extra Centers
papers.abstract: In uniform capacitated $(k,z)$-clustering, we open $k$ centers and assign every client to a center so that no center serves more than $U$ clients, minimizing the sum of the $z$-th powers of the assignment distances; $k$-median and $k$-means are the cases $z=1$ and $z=2$. We study algorithms that may open $k+\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and must respect the capacities exactly. In low dimensions, we give deterministic algorithms that are, except for $k$-median in the plane, the first polynomial-time algorithms with $(1+\varepsilon)k$ centers whose ratio is bounded independently of $\varepsilon$. In Euclidean space of any dimension, with clients of bounded doubling dimension, the ratio is $\mathcal{B}_z-(\mathcal{B}_z-1)\varepsilon+δ$ for every fixed $δ>0$, where $\mathcal{B}_z<3^z$ for $z>1$; this is $3-2\varepsilon+δ$ for $k$-median and $5-4\varepsilon+δ$ for $k$-means. In doubling metrics, the ratio is $3^z-(3^z-1)\varepsilon+δ$ when centers may share a location, and a constant otherwise, such as $\min\{7-4\varepsilon,\,3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)\}+δ$ for $k$-median. In general metrics, deleting centers greedily gives ratio $3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)+δ$ for $k$-median when centers may share a location and $7+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)+δ$ otherwise, improving the previous $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Our main tool is a rescue lemma. Splitting a near-optimal uncapacitated solution gives at most $2k-1$ blocks of at most $U$ clients, and giving a block a private center saves its share of the extra cost of following an optimal solution. Since a center of the optimal solution can be closed once all its blocks are rescued, $\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ extra centers save almost an $\varepsilon$-fraction of this extra cost instead of an $\varepsilon/2$-fraction.

papers.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
papers.abstract: We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-γ)n})$, for a fixed $γ>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.

papers.title: Strongly explicit Ramanujan 2-lift towers via Hilbert modular forms
papers.abstract: Expander graphs have been central objects of study for over fifty years. Ramanujan graphs attain the asymptotically optimal nontrivial adjacency-eigenvalue threshold for infinite fixed-degree families. The original arithmetic constructions by Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak (1988) and Margulis (1988), and the iterative $2$-lift method of Bilu-Linial (2006) provide different approaches to Ramanujan graph constructions. Motivated by work on Mealy automata, we combine both approaches to give the following new arithmetic construction. For every prime $p\equiv 1\pmod {17}$, we construct a infinite tower of $(p+1)$-regular non-bipartite Ramanujan graphs on $2^n$ vertices, with label-preserving $2$-lifts between consecutive levels. These construction is strongly explicit: for fixed $p$, a neighbor or lift sign is computable in $O_p(n^3)$ bit operations. The construction uses fixed algebraic $2$-adic transformations, specified by finite data computable in preprocessing depending only on $p$. The main number-theoretic tool is Blasius's Ramanujan-Petersson theorem for Hilbert modular forms, applied through the Jacquet-Langlands correspondence to obtain the sharp bound $|λ|\leq2\sqrt p$ for every nontrivial adjacency eigenvalue of our $(p+1)$-regular graphs. The transformations preserve $2$-adic distance, which gives the binary covers and an explicit formula for their signings.

papers.title: Random ($\log{n}$)-CNF Formulas Are Hard for Depth-$2$ Frege with Modular Gates

papers.title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
papers.abstract: We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $β=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$α< α_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings. Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms. To establish our results, we first develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, which resolves short-cycle fluctuations in the complex plane by lifting classical small subgraph conditioning on random regular graphs to random holomorphic functions. Second, we overcome the standard second-moment barrier caused by the exponential blowup of the bare second moment inside the replica-symmetric phase, by showing that replica symmetry implies a nonpositive Bethe functional and upgrading planted overlap concentration to an exponentially small bound, which enables a typical-graph truncation that controls complex second moments up to the replica symmetry breaking threshold.

papers.title: Exact Competitive Ratios of Index Rules for Scheduling with Obligatory Testing
papers.abstract: We revisit scheduling with obligatory testing, where each job consists of two operations: a test with an initially known time and an operation whose processing time is revealed upon completion of the job's test. We develop an iterative competitive-ratio-preserving instance-reduction method that enables us to compute exact competitive ratios directly on highly structured instances for various index rules. Our main result is a clean analysis showing that the competitive ratio of the algorithm $1$-SORT is exactly the Golden Ratio $\varphi\approx 1.618$, improving the recent best-known upper bound of $1.861$ for arbitrary testing times. We further leverage this method to obtain near-tight bounds for a simple randomized algorithm on instances with uniform testing times.

papers.title: Building On Learning-Augmented Online Sorting
papers.abstract: Online sorting is a problem that has gained attention recently, and is a natural translation of sorting into an online setting. The problem at hand is to place elements of an online sequence immediately and irrevocably with the goal of producing an array that is as close to sorted as possible upon inserting all elements. Recent work by Bercea et al. [ESA 2026] introduced the incorporation of learned predictions into the online sorting domain. They show lower bounds for the consistency and robustness of any algorithm, including randomization, then provide a deterministic algorithm that is $O(n/r)$-consistent and $O(r)$-robust, which are tight bounds. However, this algorithm requires prior knowledge of the optimal offline cost of the full input sequence before all elements have been revealed. We resolve this by providing an algorithm with matching bounds that does not require knowledge of the optimal cost, then extend these results to the more general problem of online metric TSP, in line with the prior work.

papers.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
papers.abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.

papers.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
papers.abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

papers.title: On the Quantum Chromatic Gap II
papers.abstract: We confirm a conjecture of the first author [SODA'26] on a strong form of pseudo-telepathy for Khot's $d$-to-$1$ games: for every $d\geq 4$, every $ε>0$, and every $k\in\mathbb N$, there is a $d$-to-$1$ label-cover game of classical value less than $ε$ that admits a perfect quantum strategy using finite-dimensional shared entanglement with measurement contexts of radius at least $k$. As a consequence, there exist graphs whose quantum chromatic number $χ_q$ is $3$ and whose classical chromatic number $χ$ is arbitrarily large. This is the first improvement on the quantum chromatic gap since the work of Brassard, Cleve, and Tapp [Phys. Rev. Lett.'99], which produced graphs for which $χ$ grows exponentially in $χ_q$. To prove the conjecture, we proceed as follows. We start with a ``stretched'' version of the Mermin--Peres magic square, obtained by spacing out its equations and linking them with additional long equation wires. This operation increases the radius of the initial measurement contexts of a perfect quantum strategy for the game, while preserving classical unsatisfiability. We then apply parallel repetition to make the classical value small, and we turn the system into a pseudo-telepathic multi-layered Kneser hypergraph via a PCP construction of Dinur, Guruswami, Khot, and Regev [STOC'03]. Finally, we feed the resulting hypergraph into the reduction of Fei, Minzer, and Wang from hypergraph colouring to $4$-to-$1$ games, we establish quantum completeness of this reduction, and we show that it preserves context radius.

papers.title: Minimum Label $k$-Cut on Planar Graphs: Complexity and Color Structure
papers.abstract: Minimum Label $k$-Cut asks for a minimum-size set of colors such that deleting all edges of these colors leaves at least $k$ connected components. We study how the structure of the underlying graph and its color classes affects the complexity of this problem. Regarding fixed-parameter tractability with respect to $k$ on simple planar graphs, we prove that the problem is W[1]-hard, even when the underlying graph is a cactus graph and each color appears at most twice. Furthermore, for cactus graphs in which every color class is connected, we establish a complexity boundary in terms of the maximum monochromatic degree: when this degree is at most two, an optimal solution can be found in $O(Nk^2)$ time, where $N$ is the input size, with no restriction on color frequency or the number of blocks spanned by a color; allowing the maximum monochromatic degree to increase to three already makes the decision version NP-complete. Finally, we prove that the problem remains W[1]-hard parameterized by $k$ on fan graphs, even when every color class is an induced path. These results show that bounding color frequency does not suffice to eliminate parameterized hardness. They also establish a monochromatic-degree boundary for connected colors on cactus graphs and identify complexity barriers to extending this tractable case to outerplanar graphs.

papers.title: Directed Cut-Query Complexity of Finding a King
papers.abstract: A king in a tournament is a vertex from which every other vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two. We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a king when a query specifies a set of vertices and returns the number of edges directed from that set to its complement. We prove that this complexity is $Θ(n)$ for $n$-vertex tournaments. To show this, we first show that every correct deterministic algorithm in this model must output a maximum-outdegree vertex, even though a king need not have maximum outdegree. We then give an adversary whose answers, after too few queries, remain consistent with a tournament in which the algorithm's output does not have maximum outdegree.

Each mediator chooses a randomized flow allocation to minimize its population's expected travel cost, subject to users having no conditional expected gain above a tolerance $ε$ from disregarding their recommendations. We define a fragmented obedient equilibrium (FOE) by combining user obedience with mediator optimality, and establish existence under a lower-hemicontinuity assumption on the obedient policy correspondences. Under affine edge latencies and independent mediator sampling, we derive an exact reformulation in first and second flow moments that preserves best responses and equilibrium profiles. Every feasible moment pair admits a finitely supported realizing policy. When the network has at most four routes, each mediator's best-response problem is an exact semidefinite program. A numerical illustration on the Braess network shows that relaxing obedience can reduce FOE costs, while gaps relative to the social optimum and optimal obedient pooling can persist.

papers.title: Certified Small Well-Separated Pair Decompositions in Practice
papers.abstract: Given n points and $ε>0$, a well-separated pair decomposition (WSPD) is a collection of dumbbells {X,Y}, where X and Y have diameter at most $ε$ times their distance, such that every pair of points has one point in X and the other in Y for some dumbbell. A partition WSPD covers every pair exactly once, and a cover WSPD at least once. Callahan and Kosaraju give a partition WSPD with $O(n/ε^d)$ dumbbells in $R^d$, but many point sets have far smaller WSPDs of both kinds. For $d\ge2$, the known $O(1)$-approximations of the minimum size WSPD that preserve the separation $ε$ have unspecified factors, above $10^7$ for $d=2$ by our estimates. For cover WSPDs, we give an $O(n^2\log n)$-time sweep approximation algorithm with a factor 40 in the plane for $ε\le1/16$. It extends to $R^d$ with a factor $2^{O(d)}$. The sweep is also a lower-bound tool: its number of steps is a lower bound on the WSPD size. For partition WSPDs, we analyze quadtree and fair split tree constructions: in the plane and for $ε\le1/5$, they give constant approximation factors, the smallest of which is 252 for a randomly shifted and scaled quadtree. In experiments with $ε=1/20$, the number of sweep steps is at least 0.91 OPT for n = 500, where the optimum OPT is known, and a local search raises it to a lower bound of 0.99 OPT. A greedy variant of the sweep, which is still a certified 40-approximation, is at most 1.28 times the lower bound for n = 10000. Followed by a new local-search heuristic that shrinks the WSPD, it is within 0.02% of the optimum on every instance with n = 500, and at most 1.10 times the lower bound for n = 10000. We then show how to convert the cover WSPDs into partition WSPDs. For n = 10000, the conversion gives on average 1.13 times the lower bound, against 1.05 for the cover WSPD itself and 1.55 for the Callahan-Kosaraju partition WSPD.

papers.title: Mathematics and Efficiency of Song's CVP Hardness Reduction
papers.abstract: Song (2026) proves that, for every fixed $0<ε<1$, the closest codeword problem (CCP) for binary linear codes under Hamming distance is NP-hard to approximate within $N^{1-ε}$, where $N$ is the code length, under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The code-to-lattice construction gives hardness within $N^{1/2-ε/2}$ for Euclidean CVP, with the same $N$ aslattice rank. This reaches every fixed Euclidean hardness exponent below one half. Aharonov and Regev (2005), with the constant refined by Gao (2026), place GapCVP at factor $cN^{1/2}$ in $\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}$ for every fixed $c>2/(π\sqrt3)\approx0.3676$. NP-hardness at that scale would imply $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$. This paper has two goals: to explain Song's theorem and its mathematics for graduate students, and to make the reduction more efficient. The reduction turns satisfiability into a system of quadratic equations and then into CCP for binary linear codes, and recovers assignments from recurrence relations of algebraic moments. We adapt the method to linear codes over any fixed finite field of characteristic $p$. A common recurrence for each block column gives a moment window $L=c_p(κ-1)+1$, where $c_p=\max\{2,p-1\}$ and $κ$ is the rank cutoff. Together with ordinary digit products and flexible sampling, this reduces interpolation degrees and output lengths. For CCP gap $N^{1-ε}$, our explicit schedule gives code length and lattice rank at most $n^{4/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$; Song's prescribed binary schedule gives $n^{8/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$. Here $n$ counts variables in a common quadratic system, equal to the number of original variables plus clauses for 3SAT. These are dimension bounds, not optimality claims or running-time exponents. The limiting hardness exponents remain Song's.

papers.title: Witnessed Boolean Contracts: Sound Local Distance Guarantees for Approximate Implicit CSG
papers.abstract: Hard min/max operations preserve the sign of exact implicit solids but generally destroy signed-distance semantics. Arbitrarily small, sign-preserving value perturbations can rotate the normalized gradient by nearly a right angle and displace a gradient-projected boundary witness by a finite amount. We formalize this as the absence of a value-only stability modulus for witness projection. We introduce a witnessed Boolean contract checking value and gradient errors, positive reach, active-branch separation, and a Lipschitz visibility margin at the approximate witness. A sharp normalization lemma bounds the normal-direction error. An enlarged neighborhood permits transfer of the inactive operand's bound between the approximate witness and the true foot point. Under the stated analytic and domain assumptions, passing the checks identifies a true point on the union boundary and bounds distance deficiency by the active operand's pointwise value error. Failed or unavailable checks return Unknown. The argument extends to finite hard unions by testing every inactive operand. An executable proof-chain audit finds no violations on 75,738 certified samples. A broader analytic stress test covers spheres, capsules, ring tori, three Boolean operators, and a four-leaf union. Of 96,000 narrow-band samples, 87,469 pass with zero oracle violations; per-case coverage ranges from 72.67% to 98.30%. Removing visibility admits 75 truly invalid witnesses, showing that branch separation alone is insufficient. Non-union cases remain empirical tests, not new theorems.

papers.title: Retrieval Sequencing in a Compact Storage System with Side Access
papers.abstract: In a compact storage system with side access, bins are arranged in adjacent vertical stacks. In each retrieval cycle, bins blocking access are lifted to create a temporary tunnel through which a robot extracts one requested bin from the side. The lifted bins are then lowered again, and the energy expenditure of the cycle equals the number of lifted bins. Given a pick list known in advance, we seek a retrieval order that minimizes total energy expenditure. For every number of stacks, we prove that the total energy separates into an instance constant and a pairwise penalty, and that every energy-optimal order is laminar within each stack. For two stacks, we prove that the retrieval sequencing problem is solvable in polynomial time. For three stacks, we give an exact polynomial-time reduction to a merge problem and characterize which merge-problem instances arise from the storage model. We define a recursive class of retrieval orders and construct a polynomial-time dynamic program that minimizes energy expenditure over this class. Finally, we quantify the additional energy savings from batching, which allows several requested bins to be retrieved in one cycle.

papers.title: Counting approximate breakpoint medians of random genomes
papers.abstract: Unsigned linear unichromosomal genomes with genes labeled 1, . . . , n are represented by permutations of these labels, whose adjacencies are the unordered pairs of genes occurring consecutively. The breakpoint distance counts the adjacencies of one genome that are absent from the other, and a breakpoint median minimizes the total breakpoint distance to a given set of genomes. Deciding whether a permutation is a median often requires a minimization over the whole symmetric group, which makes the median set resistant to exact counting. We replace this global condition by a local one: a c-approximate median is a genome having at most c adjacencies absent from all the input genomes. For a fixed genome we introduce its approximate median inverse, the set of ordered k-tuples of genomes ad- mitting it as a c-approximate median, and we construct and count this set explicitly. For k genomes chosen uniformly and independently at random, this gives the probability that a given genome is a c-approximate median and the expected number of such approximate medians. The relaxation is not only technical: approximate medians and near-optimal genomes co- incide up to a shift of the tolerance that remains bounded in probability as the number of genes grows. Finally, we derive an explicit upper bound on the probability that a given genome is an exact median, and on the expected number of exact breakpoint medians.

papers.title: The Value of Experiments in Assortment Optimization
papers.abstract: Retailers can learn customer preferences by experimenting with different assortments. However, the cost of each experiment and the operational burden of repeatedly changing product offerings can make extensive experimentation impractical. We study how much a retailer can improve its final assortment decision using customer observations from one (or a very small number of) fixed experimental assortments. We consider the multinomial logit model, where product revenues are known but customer preferences are unknown. In this setting, we jointly design the experimental assortment and the rule for selecting a final assortment from observed customer choices to minimize worst-case regret: the expected revenue loss of the final assortment relative to an optimal assortment under the true preferences, maximized over possible customer preferences. We first characterize exactly the minimax regret and an optimal assortment when no experimentation is possible. We then show, surprisingly, that offering a single experimental assortment to just one customer can already substantially reduce regret, depending on how the products' revenues compare. We derive the exact minimax regret and an optimal experimental policy in this setting. When a single fixed experimental assortment is offered to many customers, we give a geometric characterization of the limiting minimax regret and construct an asymptotically optimal policy. Depending on product revenues, this single experiment can yield no improvement over no experimentation or nearly complete regret reduction. Finally, we extend our analysis to multiple experimental assortments chosen in advance, characterizing the limiting minimax regret, constructing asymptotically optimal policies, and identifying which collections of assortments allow worst-case regret to vanish as the number of customer observations grows.

papers.title: When Imputation Changes the Nearest Neighbor: Exact Certification of Similarity Retrieval for Incomplete Sensor Time Series
papers.abstract: Sensor time series routinely reach similarity search with missing values, and the retrieved neighbours then depend on how the gaps were filled. We ask which retrieval conclusions hold for every admissible completion of an incomplete query. For a family of window-minimum distances that contains the $L_1$ distance as its separable end we give a pairwise certificate that one candidate is strictly closer than another, a guaranteed candidate set that contains every possible nearest neighbour, and a certificate that a nearest-neighbour label cannot change. The guarantees hold uniformly over the specified box and apply to the true query whenever it lies inside. At the separable end a closed form is known, but beyond it the worst-case gap need not be attained at a corner of the box. We prove a finite reduction to critical values, give an exact interval dynamic programme for the worst-case ranking gap, and a quadratic-time fast layer of valid bounds and feasible witnesses, supported by an exact criterion for when the feature-box relaxation is tight. On three traffic-sensor collections with real gap patterns, linear interpolation changes the nearest neighbour in 15 to 33 percent of the queries. At the full band the feature-box relaxation misses up to 14 percent of the exactly stable boundary pairs, whereas fixed-completion and Monte Carlo checks issue false certificates. The fast layer resolves about 90 percent of all tested boundary pairs without dynamic programming, and on paired network-scale queries the exact method is 82 to 110 times faster than the programme alone. Label certificates transfer to three public benchmarks, and the band width trades forecasting accuracy and certification coverage for lower imputation sensitivity, with dataset-dependent crossovers.

papers.title: Cubic lower bounds for the permanent in odd characteristic, for Pfaffian representations, and for polynomial entries
papers.abstract: The determinantal complexity of a polynomial is the order of the smallest matrix whose entries are polynomials of degree at most one and whose determinant equals the polynomial. A lower bound for the permanent in this measure is the algebraic form of the question whether the permanent is harder to compute than the determinant. Over the complex numbers, the best known lower bound grows cubically in the size of the permanent. It holds even when the permanent only has to be a limit of such determinants. I prove that the cubic lower bound holds over every algebraically closed field of odd characteristic $p$, with a constant that depends on $p$. Hence the cubic bound does not depend on characteristic zero. I also prove the bound for Pfaffians, which are square roots of determinants of skew symmetric matrices. Lower bounds for Pfaffians imply the same bounds for determinants. Further, I prove the bound, divided by $a$, for matrices whose entries are polynomials of degree at most $a$. All three results come from one lower bound for smooth hypersurfaces. I prove it in every characteristic by counting intersection points together with their multiplicities.
papers.comment: 18 pages; stand-alone; submitted to International Mathematical Research Notices

papers.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Non-Splitting Coflow Scheduling in Heterogeneous Parallel Networks via Iterative Relaxation
papers.abstract: Coflows capture the collective communication requirements of data-parallel applications, and scheduling them well is essential to the performance of modern data centers. We study non-splitting coflow scheduling in a heterogeneous parallel network whose $m$ network cores may be Electronic Packet Switches (EPS), not-all-stop Optical Circuit Switches (OCS), or all-stop OCS, where every flow must be transmitted entirely through a single core. Previous approximation algorithms for this setting have guarantees that grow linearly with the number of cores $m$ or with the maximum flow degree $τ$ of a port, and therefore become weak as data centers deploy more cores. The source of this dependence is the rounding step: rounding each flow to the core holding its largest fractional value can inflate the load of a port by a factor of $m$. We replace this step with an iterative relaxation rounding scheme that handles the input-port and output-port capacity constraints simultaneously. For minimizing the makespan, this yields approximation ratios of $\min\{τ, 3\}$, $2\min\{τ, 3\}$, and $4\min\{τ, 3\}$ for pure EPS, pure not-all-stop OCS, and pure all-stop OCS networks, respectively. For minimizing the total weighted coflow completion time, we obtain approximation ratios of $8\min\{τ, 4\}$, $16\min\{τ, 4\}$, and $32\min\{τ, 4\}$ for the same three architectures. In a hybrid network, the guarantee is governed by the weakest architecture present, so the overall ratios are at most $4\min\{τ,3\}\le 12$ and $32\min\{τ,4\}\le 128$, respectively. Unlike all previous guarantees for non-splitting coflow scheduling in heterogeneous parallel networks, these bounds are absolute constants that do not grow with the number of cores $m$ or with the flow degree $τ$. We also show that the integrality gap of the underlying linear program is at least $2$.

papers.title: Diagonalization and Undecidability in Semi-Thue Systems
papers.abstract: We revisit classical diagonalization argument in the setting of semi-Thue systems, viewing computation as nondeterministic rewriting rather than sequential machine execution. Semi-Thue systems naturally generate derivation trees, making existential acceptance, reachability, and infinite derivations fundamental computational notions. We formulate acceptance and decision directly in terms of derivation trees and study the associated assertion, word, and infiniteness problems. We prove that the complements of the assertion and word problems are not recursively enumerable by direct Post-style diagonal arguments. For the infiniteness problem, we give a constructive diagonalization based on a fixed universal semi-Thue system. Unlike the classical approach, the diagonal construction is carried out entirely within the rewriting formalism: the universal system remains an ordinary nondeterministic semi-Thue system while simulating encoded semi-Thue computations, including self-reference. These results show that undecidability in semi-Thue systems arises naturally from universality and self-reference in nondeterministic rewriting, rather than from machine states or control mechanisms. This perspective clarifies the relationship between rewriting systems, recursive enumerability, and classical diagonal arguments originating in the work of Post and Turing.

papers.title: Finding Competitive Equilibria in Online Marketplaces with Platform Fees, Taxes, and Subsidies
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium computation in multi-unit trading networks with valuations satisfying generalized full substitutes and agent- and transaction-specific piecewise-linear transfer functions. These transfers model platform fees, taxes, subsidies, and membership discounts in online marketplaces. Our ascending procedure raises prices at different rates and reaches the minimum equilibrium price vector in finitely many iterations, each implementable in strongly polynomial time under our oracle and arithmetic models. An equilibrium allocation can then be recovered efficiently. The method extends primal-dual techniques developed for ascending auctions to handle complementarities between purchases and sales through a submodular flow formulation. In single-seller markets with substitutes and complements, our framework also extends the double-track auctions of Sun and Yang (2009) and Shioura and Yang (2015) to bidder- and good-specific transfers.

papers.title: From Trees to Binary Trees: Approximation Algorithms and a PTAS
papers.abstract: Kellerhals, Krebs, Nichterlein, and Schmid introduced the optimization problem Tree in Binary Tree (TBT), where, given a tree $T$, the task is to find a binary tree $S^*$ with $V(T)=V(S^*)$ that minimizes $\sum_{uv\in E(T)} \operatorname{dist}_{S^*}(u,v)$. They also introduced the variant Tree in Binary Tree With Steiner Nodes (TBT-SN), where the condition $V(T)=V(S^*)$ is relaxed to $V(T)\subseteq V(S^*)$. We give a simple linear-time $\frac{8}{3}$-approximation algorithm for TBT and a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for TBT-SN. Our main building idea in both algorithms is to iteratively consider subtrees of the tree $T$ which contain all vertices below some vertex $v$ and construct a solution where $v$ has degree 1. For the PTAS, we cut $T$ into smaller trees, solve these instances, modify the obtained solutions, and combine them to achieve a solution for the original instance.

papers.title: One Polynomial Field for Every Euler Step and the Flow: Polynomial Dynamics for P and PSPACE
papers.abstract: We construct, for each deterministic Turing machine that halts on all inputs, one polynomial vector field with rational coefficients that performs the same logical computation at unit Euler step, at every smaller or variable step in $(0,1]$ with divergent sum, and along the flow. This unifies discrete-time and continuous-time computation by polynomial dynamics, which earlier characterizations treated separately. For a machine making $T$ transitions in space $H$, a logical scale $h=2^{-s}$ with $s=O(H)$ suffices, with physical time $O(s(T+s))$, drift disturbances up to $h^{2K}$ for a fixed exponent $K$, and $2Ks+3$ fractional bits at unit step. On a fixed compact domain, polynomial time and robust eventual decision characterize P and PSPACE, respectively, with polynomial scale thresholds and no supplied stabilization horizon in the space case. Without sign, floor or conditional primitives, margin amplification at bounded speed, overlapping polynomial gates and interval-product estimates give the common realization, from which we derive shared logical traces, fixed-field PSPACE-complete prediction and a robust safety family with polynomial certificates common to all Euler steps and the flow.
papers.comment: 93 pages. Ancillary files: exact local checks (Python 3, standard library only)

papers.title: Parameterized Approximation of Max k-Weight CSP: A Dichotomy for Boolean Languages
papers.abstract: We study \textsc{Max $k$-Weight CSP}: maximize the satisfied weight of Boolean constraints with nonnegative rational weights by setting at most $k$ variables to $1$. Each constraint uses at most $d$ distinct variables and a relation from a finite Boolean language $Γ$. This includes \textsc{Partial Vertex Cover}, \textsc{Densest $k$-Subgraph}, bounded-frequency \textsc{Maximum Coverage}, and cardinality-constrained \textsc{Max-SAT}. We completely classify the fixed finite languages admitting an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) with parameter $k+d$. Only nonempty relations excluding the all-zero tuple matter. For such a relation, a coordinate is a \emph{unit witness} if the tuple with a single $1$ in that coordinate is accepted, and a \emph{control} otherwise. A relation is \emph{Direct} if setting any selected control to $0$, with all other coordinates unchanged, preserves satisfaction. It is \emph{Rooted} if every satisfying tuple has a selected unit witness such that keeping it, setting all other unit witnesses to $0$, and setting any subset of selected controls to $0$ preserves satisfaction. If all such relations are Direct, or all are Rooted, we give a deterministic $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for every rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ in time $2^{O(d+k\log(1+dk/\varepsilon))}\ell_{\mathrm{in}}^{O(1)}$, where $\ell_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the total input length. The algorithms are uniform in $d$ and give an EPAS parameterized by $k+d$ whenever relation membership is polynomial-time decidable. If neither condition holds, no EPAS exists unless $\mathsf{FPT}=\mathsf{W[1]}$, even for unweighted instances where no two constraints involve the same set of variables.

papers.title: Quantum Query Complexity of Tournament Solutions
papers.abstract: A tournament solution records a set of winners from a tournament, that is, from the outcomes of all pairwise comparisons among $N$ alternatives. We study the quantum query complexity of computing tournament solutions when the outcome of each comparison has to be learned by a query. Classically, the picture is uniform: the Copeland set, the uncovered set and the top cycle all require $Θ(N^2)$ queries, and so does finding a single vertex of maximum out-degree. We show that the quantum query complexity of the top cycle can be computed with $\tildeΘ(N)$ queries, and a Condorcet winner can be found with $\tilde Θ(\sqrt N)$ queries. Finding a strong king requires $Θ(N^{3/2})$ queries, the same as finding a vertex of maximum out-degree. We also give a self-contained alternative proof of the known $Θ(N^{3/2})$ bound for finding a vertex of maximum degree, established by Gilani, Mande, Patro, and Raja. Our lower bounds reduce counting problems to tournament problems using Ambainis's adversary method. For the top cycle, we find a Hamiltonian path and locate the prefix forming the top cycle by divide and conquer.

papers.title: Layering and reverse extension for weighted $k$-path vertex cover
papers.abstract: We study the weighted $k$-path vertex cover problem for any fixed integer $k \ge 2$, in which a vertex non-negatively weighted simple graph $G = (V, E)$ is given and one wants to find a minimum-weight vertex subset $C \subseteq V$ such that every simple path on $k$ vertices in $G$ contains at least one vertex of $C$. The problem generalizes the classic weighted vertex cover problem, that is, $k = 2$, and it admits a $k$-approximation algorithm of Hochbaum~[SIAM J. Comput., 1982] and a $(k - \frac 12)$-approximation algorithm of Brüstle et al.~[IWOCA 2021]. In this paper, we carefully design local weight functions in the Layering and Reverse Extension local ratio framework of Bar-Yehuda et al.~[ACM Comput. Surv., 2004], leading to an approximation algorithm of ratio $\frac {3k-1}4$ for odd $k \ge 3$ and of ratio $\frac {3k}4$ for even $k \ge 4$. When $k = 3$ and $k = 4$, these ratios are $2$ and $3$, respectively, matching the state-of-the-art approximation ratios for the corresponding special cases.

papers.title: Optimal self-orthogonal binary linear codes
papers.abstract: We complete the determination of the minimum possible length of eight-dimensional binary self-orthogonal codes with given minimum distance. For dimension nine we give exact values and bounds for minimum distance at most $64$. By exploiting the geometric reformulation of linear codes as multisets of points, we fully redo the classification for dimension at most seven in a simplified and computer-free manner. As a by-product we prove the non-existence of $[93,9,44]_2$ codes and show several divisibility results for putative optimal nine-dimensional binary codes.

papers.title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
papers.abstract: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.
papers.comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. JEL: C73, G14, G41

papers.title: Local Convergence of Triadic Closures of Sparse Random Graphs
papers.abstract: Triadic closure is a natural mechanism for modeling the clustering phenomenon observed in many real-world networks. Given a possibly random undirected graph $H$, we consider pairs of non-adjacent vertices that have a common neighbor. Conditional on $H$, each such pair is joined by an edge independently and simultaneously, with a probability depending on the degrees of its endpoints and on the number of their common neighbors. The resulting graph is called a triadic closure of $H$. We study the effect of this operation on local convergence. More precisely, we prove that if a sequence of potentially random finite undirected graphs of $\left( H_n \right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges locally in probability to a rooted graph $H^*$, then the corresponding sequence of triadic closures converges locally in probability to the same triadic closure of $H^*$. As a consequence, we obtain a general limit theorem for the clustering coefficients of triadic closures. In particular, we show that the triadic closures can have a strictly positive limiting clustering coefficients even when the limiting clustering coefficients of the parent graph sequence is zero. Finally, we apply our results to several classical sparse random graph models including Erdős-Rényi, configuration, preferential attachment models and compute the limiting clustering coefficients of their triadic closures.

papers.title: What Can Be Computed with Indefinite Causal Structure?
papers.abstract: Can quantum computation become more powerful when operations do not need to follow a definite causal order? We study this question in the process matrix formalism of Oreshkov et al. (Nature Communications, 2012), which allows quantum operations to be connected without a fixed global order. In the computational model, a quantum circuit succinctly describes a process matrix, and the algorithm is given access to its generated channel, with computational cost measured by the size of the generating circuit. We give polynomial-time algorithms in two settings. First, general process matrix computation suffices to solve every problem in $\textbf{NP}$. The valid processes used by our algorithm satisfy the purification postulate of Araújo et al. (Quantum, 2017), and their generated channels are unitary, although their generating circuits are not. Second, requiring the process matrices themselves to be pure, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for unique-sink orientation, a general problem capturing several longstanding computational problems in optimization. Our unitary generators are constructed explicitly and efficiently. Assuming that unique-sink orientation has no quantum polynomial-time algorithm, our result shows that indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond $\textbf{BQP}$ within the process matrix formalism, even while preserving unitarity.

papers.title: On edge-ordered Ramsey numbers of hypergraphs
papers.abstract: For an integer $h\geq2$, an edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $H^<$ is an $h$-uniform hypergraph with a linear ordering of its hyperedges. For an integer $q \geq 1$, the edge-ordered Ramsey number $R_{\mathrm{edge}}(H^<;q)$ of $H^<$ is the smallest positive integer $N$ such that there exists an edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $G^<$ on $N$ vertices such that, for every $q$-coloring of the hyperedges of $G^<$, there is a monochromatic copy of $H^<$ in $G^<$ preserving the hyperedge order. In this note, we show that, for every edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $F^<$ on $n$ vertices with $m\geq1$ hyperedges, $R_{\mathrm{edge}}(F^<;q) \leq R_h(F;q)^{Cm^2}$ where $F$ is the underlying unordered hypergraph, $R_h(F;q)$ is its standard $q$-color Ramsey number, and $C=C(h,q)>0$ is a constant. For fixed $h\geq3$ and $q\geq2$, this shows that prescribing the hyperedge order does not require an increase in the tower height of the classical upper bound. It also settles a problem posed by Fox and Li (2020), and for $h=2$ gives the bound $2^{O(n^4\log n)}$, improving their bounds for every fixed $q \geq 3$.

papers.title: Substring Complexity in BWT-Runs Bounded Space
papers.abstract: Given a string $T[1..n]$, its substring complexity is defined as $δ=\max_k d_k/k$, where $d_k$ is the number of its distinct substrings of length $k$ in $T$. We show how to compute it in $O(n+r\log r)$ time, using only $O(r)$ words of space, where $r$ denotes the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform.

papers.title: Compressed Orientation Reachability Maps for Sub-Second Robotic Needle Entry Point Planning
papers.abstract: In the context of multi-stage trajectory planning for robotic percutaneous liver interventions, identifying a kinematically feasible entry point remains a critical computational bottleneck. Existing methods rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics or randomized searches, incurring delays of 13 to 27 seconds per target and limiting real-time intraoperative adaptation. This paper introduces an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) that precomputes the kinematic feasibility of a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator across 188,873 workspace positions and encodes orientation feasibility into a compact, indexed 83 MB map. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled runtime pipeline replaces live optimization with near-instantaneous array lookups. Experimental evaluation demonstrates a reduction in planning latency from 13.5-26.9 s to 0.289-0.349 s per target while maintaining high geometric fidelity, achieving a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933 and a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 relative to the baseline reachable point cloud. The proposed ORM framework enables sub-second entry point planning and provides an efficient computational framework for robotic needle insertion in percutaneous liver ablation.

papers.title: EPPA for Reducts of the Random Graph
papers.abstract: We prove that finite two-graphs have coherent EPPA and that neither graphs modulo global complementation nor two-graphs modulo global complementation have EPPA. This completes the classification of EPPA and coherent EPPA for the reducts of the random graph, answering a question and confirming a conjecture of Evans, Hubička, Konečný and Nešetřil.

papers.title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
papers.abstract: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

papers.title: Reachability in Five-Dimensional Vector Addition Systems Is PSPACE-Complete
papers.abstract: Vector addition systems (VAS) are a fundamental model of concurrent computation in which transitions update nonnegative integer counters by adding integer vectors, provided all counters remain nonnegative. Closely related to Petri nets, VAS are the single-state counterpart of vector addition systems with states (VASS), which use finitely many states to restrict the available transitions. A classical simulation of $d$-VASS by $(d+3)$-VAS connects their reachability problems, but the complexity-theoretic picture of fixed-dimensional VAS remains largely unclear. While reachability in $2$-VASS is PSPACE-complete under binary encoding, the best known upper bound for $5$-VAS was only elementary. We prove that every reachable $5$-VAS instance has a reachability witness of length polynomial in its unary size. Consequently, $5$-VAS reachability is NL-complete under unary encoding and PSPACE-complete under binary encoding. We also establish a polynomial factorization of the reachability relation of every $d$-VAS with $d \ge 3$. For $5$-VAS, this strengthens Hopcroft and Pansiot's effective semilinearity of reachability sets to the full reachability relation. For every fixed $d\ge3$, it also yields an $\mathsf F_d$ upper bound for reachability in $(d+3)$-VAS.

papers.title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers
papers.abstract: In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

papers.title: An Exact Parallel Dense Gauss-Seidel Algorithm with Trade-Offs between Parallel Execution Time and Preprocessing Time
papers.abstract: The Gauss-Seidel iterative method is commonly used for solving systems of linear equations because of its good convergence properties. However, the Gauss-Seidel algorithm cannot be easily parallelized because of the data dependencies existing at each iteration. The best parallel execution time for dense systems of equations is $O(n)$ given that enough processors are available and no preprocessing is performed. In this paper we propose a new parallel Gauss-Seidel algorithm which is capable of achieving better parallel runtimes at the expense of more preprocessing time. The algorithm can be tuned in order to provide convenient trade-offs between the preprocessing time and the best parallel runtime achievable by the algorithm.
papers.comment: This manuscript was originally written in July 2013, and the names and affiliation of the authors are reflecting the state at that time. Recently, the original manuscript went through a few rounds of AI-based reviews, which identified several typos and bugs, which were corrected, but which didn't change the original ideas. AI was only used for identifying issues, not for correcting them

papers.title: Diameter-two graphs whose mutual-visibility chromatic number equals their chromatic number
papers.abstract: A set $S$ of vertices of a graph $G$ is a mutual-visibility set if every pair of vertices of $S$ is joined by a shortest path whose internal vertices avoid $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $χ_μ(G)$ is the least number of mutual-visibility sets into which $V(G)$ can be partitioned. Klavžar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero (2025) proved that $χ_μ(G)\leχ(G)$ whenever $G$ has diameter two, observed that equality holds for complete bipartite graphs, and asked whether there are any other diameter-two graphs attaining equality. We answer this question in the affirmative. We construct a graph $G_{11}$ of order 11 and diameter two with $χ_μ(G_{11})=χ(G_{11})=3$, and an infinite family of such graphs obtained from $G_{11}$ by replacing one vertex with pairwise non-adjacent copies of it.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to Aequationes Mathematicae

papers.title: Average pairwise Hamming distance of a subset in a hypercube
papers.abstract: In this note, we prove that for a subset $\mathcal{F}$ of $\{0,1\}^n$ of density $\frac{1}{8}$, its average pairwise Hamming distance is at least $\frac{n-3}{2}$, with equality attained only by $(n-3)$-dimensional subcubes. This answers a question of Lei Yu, and solves an important open case of a more general question posed by Ahlswede and Katona in 1977.
